So many people are hard set against discussing methods, but it seems to me that this contributes greatly to the number of people who attempt to take their life, uninformed and end up hurting themselves and dooming themselves to a life of even greater suffering. Suicide has always been a part of human existence. Should it be taboo to discuss how to decrease the potential suffering involved in the process?

I know our group is small, but I'd like to hear other thoughts on the matter.
Addressing Taboo. Let's Weigh the Pros and Cons of Discussing Methods.
Can we not discuss them here? What are the rules?
Right now the rules are free and open. I just wanted to gauge feeling.
I'm not sure how useful it is but I have no real objection.

I think there's probably a concern that discussing methods is a step closer to maybe pushing someone to go through with it. And while it's nice to be able to discuss suicide openly, there's no doubt there will be people that stumble into here who may just be going through a particularly hard time. I would be very uncomfortable knowing that I contributed to the death of someone who really hadn't thought it through.

That said, my plan is unusual enough, I reckon, to be unlikely to resonate with anyone - and I can be somewhat vague about it. As I'd want it to look like an accident, I plan on going for a very long run and basically blowing up my heart. I think it would be quite comforting for people to believe I died doing something I love.

I see it as a double edged blade. Providing methods could give someone an extra push, but not providing them could also leave a fully decided, yet functionally mistaken or misled person with a fate much worse than death.

Can blowing up your heart that way work? I would think that could just as easily lead to a non-fatal heart attack. I'm curious and sure you've thought about it much more than me.

I have given it some thought. And while it's by no means foolproof, the beauty of it is, a failed attempt should not lead to suspicion around my intent, leading to potential unwanted hospitalisation (for psychiatric reasons).

I've been running for years with a heart rate monitor so I know how much I can push the old ticker. I also know that with everyday supplements that wouldn't look at all out of place in my blood I can push it a lot harder. I also know that by depriving my body of certain things I can push it even harder. Add to that a history of heart conditions in the family and I'm pretty convinced I could do it.

Then, if I choose a sufficiently remote place to run (easy in the country I live) and go on a sufficiently hot day, I'd seriously reduce the likelihood of being found.

The one obvious downside is that it could end up being an extremely long drawn out and painful way to go and I haven't come up with a plausible way to deal with that. Best case, rush of adrenalin, heart explodes, brain shuts down. Worst case, rush of adrenalin, mild heart attack, slow death by dehydration and heatstroke.

The worst case, slow death, would be a bitch. Hopefully the heatstroke would knock you unconscious. I know high doses of ephedrine, like in otc bronchial meds can highly increase heartrate. Is this one of the supplements you mention?

the EC stack ... ephedrine and caffeine. You could do it with caffeine alone.,. In high enough doses (not even that high, actually) it's deadly and anyone can get hold of grams of pure caffeine. I've even had a few dry runs (pun intended).

But I'm having an attack of conscience at the moment.

There's actually a site that lists statistics regarding the most lethal suicide methods: http://lostallhope.com/suicide-methods/statistics-most-lethal-methods

That being said, I believe it's important for people to know the truth behind the effectiveness, pain, and most importantly potential for permanent injury from a failed suicide attempt by method. More importantly it needs to be presented in a completely objective way, without any pro or anti-suicide rhetoric. Without that objectivity and those facts suicidal people run the risk of permanently injuring themselves and leaving them worse off than they were before should they choose to go through with it. As much of a sensitive subject as it is, we cannot deal with the problem or help suicidal people if we're not willing to re-examine our positions and be open to the truth. I feel presenting the facts and being completely unbiased and non-judgmental about it would help suicidal people a lot more than trying to intimidate them with lies and hurtful rhetoric.
